summary: Common carp, which includes koi, is a pest fish that damages aquatic ecosystems in Queens. When carp feed, they root around on the bottom and uproot water plants while stirring up mud, which makes the water murky and blocks light. This destruction harms the plant-filled breeding areas that native fish and birds depend on. Removing carp from waterways has been shown to bring back more kinds of bottom-living invertebrates.
history: Common carp originally came from Eurasia. While people once thought carp arrived in the Hudson River during the 1830s, those turned out to be goldfish or goldfish hybrids instead. The first confirmed arrival of carp was in California in 1872. Beginning in 1877, the U.S. Fish Commission deliberately stocked carp across much of the country as a food fish, but people soon lost interest in them. Today carp are considered a nuisance and have been found in every state except Alaska.

handling.text: Never release aquarium or pond fish into lakes, ponds or streams. NYS DEC suggests donating unwanted fish to a school, nature center, aquarium or zoo, returning them to the store, trading them with another hobbyist, or asking a veterinarian or pet store about humane options. In New York City parks like Kissena, park rules forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest or eggs.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks like Kissena Park, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
